11✦ 2 Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “On the first day of the first month you shall raise up the tabernacle of the Tent of Meeting.2✦ 3 You shall put the ark of the covenant in it, and you shall screen the ark with the veil.✦ 4 You shall bring in the table, and set in order the things that are on it. You shall bring in the lamp stand, and light3 its lamps.✦ 5 You shall set the golden altar for incense before the ark of the covenant, and put the screen of the door to the tabernacle.4✦ 6 “You shall set the altar of burnt offering before the door of the tabernacle of the Tent of Meeting.5✦ 7 You shall set the basin between the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and shall put water6 therein.7✦ 8 You shall set up the court around it, and hang up the screen of the gate of the court.8✦ 9 “You shall take the anointing oil, and anoint the tabernacle and all that is in it, and shall make it holy9, and all its furniture, and it will be holy.10✦ 10 You shall anoint the altar of burnt offering, with all its vessels, and sanctify the altar, and the altar will be most holy11.12✦ 11 You shall anoint the basin and its base, and sanctify it.13✦ 12 “You shall bring Aaron and his sons to the door of the Tent of Meeting, and shall wash them with water14.15✦ 13 You shall put on Aaron the holy16 garments; and you shall anoint him, and sanctify him, that he may minister to me in the priest’s office.17✦ 14 You shall bring his sons, and put tunics on them.18✦ 15 You shall anoint them, as you anointed their father, that they may minister to me in the priest’s office. Their anointing shall be to them for an everlasting priesthood throughout their generations.”19✦ 16 Moses did so. According to all that Yahweh commanded him, so he did.2021✦ 17 In the first month in the second year, on the first day of the month, the tabernacle was raised up.2223✦ 18 Moses raised up the tabernacle, and laid its sockets, and set up its boards, and put in its bars, and raised up its pillars.✦ 19 He spread the covering over the tent, and put the roof of the tabernacle above on it, as Yahweh commanded Moses.2425✦ 20 He took and put the covenant into the ark, and set the poles on the ark, and put the mercy26 seat above on the ark.27✦ 21 He brought the ark into the tabernacle, and set up the veil of the screen, and screened the ark of the covenant, as Yahweh commanded Moses.2829✦ 22 He put the table in the Tent of Meeting, on the north side of the tabernacle, outside of the veil.30✦ 23 He set the bread in order on it before Yahweh, as Yahweh commanded Moses.3132✦ 24 He put the lamp stand in the Tent of Meeting, opposite the table, on the south side of the tabernacle.33✦ 25 He lit the lamps before Yahweh, as Yahweh commanded Moses.3435✦ 26 He put the golden altar in the Tent of Meeting before the veil;36✦ 27 and he burned incense of sweet spices on it, as Yahweh commanded Moses.3738✦ 28✦ 29 He put up the screen of the door to the tabernacle. He set the altar of burnt offering at the door of the tabernacle of the Tent of Meeting, and offered on it the burnt offering and the meal offering, as Yahweh commanded Moses.3940✦ 30 He set the basin between the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and put water41 therein, with which to wash.42✦ 31 Moses, Aaron, and his sons washed their hands and their feet there.43✦ 32 When they went into the Tent of Meeting, and when they came near to the altar, they washed, as Yahweh commanded Moses.4445✦ 33 He raised up the court around the tabernacle and the altar, and set up the screen of the gate of the court. So Moses finished the work.46✦ 34 Then the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and Yahweh’s glory47 filled the tabernacle48.495051✦ 35 Moses wasn’t able to enter into the Tent of Meeting52, because the cloud stayed on it, and Yahweh’s glory53 filled the tabernacle.5455✦ 36 When the cloud was taken up from over the tabernacle, the children of Israel went onward, throughout all their journeys;56✦ 37 but if the cloud wasn’t taken up, then they didn’t travel until the day that it was taken up.57✦ 38 For the cloud of Yahweh was on the tabernacle by day, and there was fire in the cloud by night, in the sight of all the house of Israel, throughout all their journeys.

12✦1 “‘If anyone sin3s, in that he hears a public adjuration to testify, he being a witness, whether he has seen or known, if he doesn’t report it, then he shall bear his iniquity.45✦ 2 “‘Or if anyone touches any unclean thing, whether it is the carcass of an unclean animal, or the carcass of unclean livestock, or the carcass of unclean creeping things, and it is hidden from him, and he is unclean, then he shall be guilty.67✦ 3 “‘Or if he touches the uncleanness of man8, whatever his uncleanness is with which he is unclean, and it is hidden from him; when he knows of it, then he shall be guilty.9✦ 4 “‘Or if anyone swears rashly with his lips to do evil or to do good10—whatever it is that a man11 might utter rashly with an oath, and it is hidden from him—when he knows of it, then he will be guilty of one of these.1213✦ 5 It shall be, when he is guilty of one of these, he shall confess that in which he has sinned;14✦ 6 and he shall bring his trespass offering to Yahweh for his sin15 which he has sinned: a female from the flock, a lamb or a goat, for a sin offering; and the priest shall make atonement16 for him concerning his sin.1718✦ 7 “‘If he can’t afford a lamb, then he shall bring his trespass offering for that in which he has sin19ned, two turtledoves, or two young pigeons20, to Yahweh; one for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering.2122✦ 8 He shall bring them to the priest, who shall first offer the one which is for the sin23 offering. 12✦134✦ 2 Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “If anyone sin5s, and commits a trespass against Yahweh, and deals falsely with his neighbor in a matter of deposit, or of bargain, or of robbery, or has oppressed his neighbor,678✦ 3 or has found that which was lost, and lied about it, and swearing to a lie—in any of these things that a man9 sins in his actions—10✦ 4 then it shall be, if he has sinned, and is guilty, he shall restore that which he took by robbery, or the thing which he has gotten by oppression, or the deposit which was committed to him, or the lost thing which he found,11✦ 5 or any thing about which he has sworn falsely: he shall restore it in full, and shall add a fifth part more to it. 1✦123 2 Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying, “When a man4 shall have a swelling in his body’s skin5, or a scab, or a bright spot, and it becomes in the skin of his body the plague of leprosy, then he shall be brought to Aaron the priest or to one of his sons, the priests.6✦ 3 The priest shall examine the plague in the skin of the body. Behold, if in his eyes the plague is arrested and the plague hasn’t spread in the skin, then the priest shall isolate him for seven more days.9✦ 6 The priest shall examine him again on the seventh day. Behold, if the plague has faded and the plague hasn’t spread in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him clean. It is a scab. He shall wash his clothes, and be clean.10✦ 7 But if the scab spreads on the skin after he has shown himself to the priest for his cleansing, he shall show himself to the priest again.11✦ 8 The priest shall examine him; and behold, if the scab has spread on the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean. It is leprosy.12✦ 9 “When the plague of leprosy is in a man13, then he shall be brought to the priest;14✦ 10 and the priest shall examine him. Behold, if there is a white swelling in the skin, and it has turned the hair white, and there is raw flesh in the swelling,15✦ 11 it is a chronic leprosy in the skin of his body, and the priest shall pronounce him unclean. He shall not isolate him, for he is already unclean.16✦ 12 “If the leprosy breaks out all over the skin, and the leprosy covers all the skin of the infected person from his head even to his feet, as far as it appears to the priest,17✦ 13 then the priest shall examine him. It has all turned white: he is clean.18✦ 14 But whenever raw flesh appears in him, he shall be unclean.19✦ 15 The priest shall examine the raw flesh, and pronounce him unclean: the raw flesh is unclean. It is leprosy.20✦ 16 Or if the raw flesh turns again, and is changed to white, then he shall come to the priest.21✦ 17 The priest shall examine him. Behold, if the plague has turned white, then the priest shall pronounce him clean of the plague. He is clean.22✦ 18 “When the body has a boil on its skin, and it has healed,23✦ 19 and in the place of the boil there is a white swelling, or a bright spot, reddish-white, then it shall be shown to the priest.24✦ 20 The priest shall examine it. Behold, if its appearance is deeper than the skin, and its hair has turned white, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean. It is the plague of leprosy. It is a plague.27✦ 23 But if the bright spot stays in its place, and hasn’t spread, it is the scar from the boil; and the priest shall pronounce him clean.28✦ 24 “Or when the body has a burn from fire on its skin, and the raw flesh of the burn becomes a bright spot, reddish-white, or white,29✦ 25 then the priest shall examine it; and behold, if the hair in the bright spot has turned white, and its appearance is deeper than the skin, it is leprosy. It has broken out in the burning, and the priest shall pronounce him unclean. It is the plague of leprosy.30✦ 26 But if the priest examines it, and behold, there is no white hair in the bright spot, and it isn’t deeper than the skin, but has faded, then the priest shall isolate him seven days.31✦ 27 The priest shall examine him on the seventh day. If it has spread in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean. It is the plague of leprosy.32✦ 28 If the bright spot stays in its place, and hasn’t spread in the skin, but is faded, it is the swelling from the burn, and the priest shall pronounce him clean, for it is the scar from the burn.33✦ 29 “When a man34 or woman35 has a plague on the head or on the beard,36✦ 30 then the priest shall examine the plague; and behold, if its appearance is deeper than the skin, and the hair in it is yellow and thin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean. It is leprosy of the head or of the beard.37✦ 31 If the priest examines the plague of itching, and behold, its appearance isn’t deeper than the skin, and there is no black hair in it, then the priest shall isolate the person infected with itching seven days.38✦ 32 On the seventh day the priest shall examine the plague; and behold, if the itch hasn’t spread, and there is no yellow hair in it, and the appearance of the itch isn’t deeper than the skin,39✦ 33 then he shall be shaved, but he shall not shave the itch. Then the priest shall isolate the one who has the itch seven more days.40✦ 34 On the seventh day, the priest shall examine the itch; and behold, if the itch hasn’t spread in the skin, and its appearance isn’t deeper than the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him clean. He shall wash his clothes and be clean.41✦ 35 But if the itch spreads in the skin after his cleansing,42✦ 36 then the priest shall examine him; and behold, if the itch has spread in the skin, the priest shall not look for the yellow hair; he is unclean.43✦ 37 But if in his eyes the itch is arrested and black hair has grown in it, then the itch is healed. He is clean. The priest shall pronounce him clean.44✦ 38 “When a man45 or a woman46 has bright spots in the skin of the body, even white bright spots,47✦ 39 then the priest shall examine them. Behold, if the bright spots on the skin of their body are a dull white, it is a harmless rash. It has broken out in the skin. He is clean.48✦ 40 “If a man49’s hair has fallen from his head, he is bald. He is clean.50✦ 41 If his hair has fallen off from the front part of his head, he is forehead bald. He is clean.51✦ 42 But if a reddish-white plague is in the bald head or the bald forehead, it is leprosy breaking out in his bald head or his bald forehead.52✦ 43 Then the priest shall examine him. Behold, if the swelling of the plague is reddish-white in his bald head, or in his bald forehead, like the appearance of leprosy in the skin of the body,53✦ 44 he is a leprous man54. He is unclean. The priest shall surely pronounce him unclean. His plague is on his head.55✦ 45 “The leper in whom the plague is shall wear torn clothes, and the hair of his head shall hang loose. He shall cover his upper lip, and shall cry, ‘Unclean! Unclean!56’5758✦ 46 All the days in which the plague is in him he shall be unclean. He is unclean. He shall dwell alone. His dwelling shall be outside of the camp.59✦ 47 “The garment also that the plague of leprosy is in, whether it is a woolen garment, or a linen garment;6061✦ 48 whether it is in warp or woof; of linen or of wool; whether in a leather, or in anything made of leather;62✦ 49 if the plague is greenish or reddish in the garment, or in the leather, or in the warp, or in the woof, or in anything made of leather; it is the plague of leprosy, and shall be shown to the priest.63✦ 50 The priest shall examine the plague, and isolate the plague seven days.64✦ 51 He shall examine the plague on the seventh day. If the plague has spread in the garment, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in the skin, whatever use the skin is used for, the plague is a destructive mildew. It is unclean.65✦ 52 He shall burn the garment, whether the warp or the woof, in wool or in linen, or anything of leather, in which the plague is, for it is a destructive mildew. It shall be burned in the fire.66✦ 53 “If the priest examines it, and behold, the plague hasn’t spread in the garment, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in anything of skin;67✦ 54 then the priest shall command that they wash the thing that the plague is in, and he shall isolate it seven more days.68✦ 55 Then the priest shall examine it, after the plague is washed; and behold, if the plague hasn’t changed its color, and the plague hasn’t spread, it is unclean; you shall burn it in the fire. It is a mildewed spot, whether the bareness is inside or outside.69✦ 56 If the priest looks, and behold, the plague has faded after it is washed, then he shall tear it out of the garment, or out of the skin, or out of the warp, or out of the woof;70✦ 57 and if it appears again in the garment, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in anything of skin, it is spreading. You shall burn what the plague is in with fire.71✦ 58 The garment, either the warp, or the woof, or whatever thing of skin it is, which you shall wash, if the plague has departed from them, then it shall be washed the second time, and it will be clean.”72✦ 59 This is the law of the plague of mildew in a garment of wool or linen, either in the warp, or the woof, or in anything of skin, to pronounce it clean, or to pronounce it unclean.

14

12✦13 2 Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “This shall be the law of the leper in the day of his cleansing: He shall be brought to the priest,4✦ 3 and the priest shall go out of the camp. The priest shall examine him. Behold, if the plague of leprosy is healed in the leper,5 4 then the priest shall command them to take for him who is to be cleansed two living clean birds, cedar wood, scarlet, and hyssop6.7✦ 5 The priest shall command them to kill one of the birds in an earthen vessel over running water8.9✦ 6 As for the living bird, he shall take it, the cedar wood, the scarlet, and the hyssop, and shall dip them and the living bird in the blood10 of the bird that was killed over the running water11.12✦ 7 He shall sprinkle on him who is to be cleansed from the leprosy seven times13, and shall pronounce him clean, and shall let the living bird go into the open field.14✦ 8 “He who is to be cleansed shall wash his clothes, and shave off all his hair, and bathe himself in water15; and he shall be clean. After that he shall come into the camp, but shall dwell outside his tent seven days.1617✦ 9 It shall be on the seventh day, that he shall shave all his hair off his head and his beard and his eyebrows. He shall shave off all his hair. He shall wash his clothes, and he shall bathe his body in water18. Then he shall be clean.19✦ 10 “On the eighth day he shall take two male lambs without defect, one ewe lamb a year old without defect, three tenths of an ephah of fine flour for a meal offering, mixed with oil, and one log of oil.202122✦ 11 The priest who cleanses him shall set the man23 who is to be cleansed, and those things, before Yahweh, at the door of the Tent of Meeting.24 12 “The priest shall take one of the male lambs, and offer him for a trespass offering, with the log of oil, and wave them for a wave offering before Yahweh.2526✦ 13 He shall kill the male lamb in the place where they kill the sin27 offering and the burnt offering, in the place of the sanctuary; for as the sin offering is the priest’s, so is the trespass offering. It is most holy28.29✦ 14 The priest shall take some of the blood30 of the trespass offering, and the priest shall put it on the tip of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot.31✦ 15 The priest shall take some of the log of oil, and pour it into the palm of his own left hand.32✦ 16 The priest shall dip his right finger in the oil that is in his left hand, and shall sprinkle some of the oil with his finger seven times before Yahweh.3334 17 The priest shall put some of the rest of the oil that is in his hand on the tip of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot, upon the blood35 of the trespass offering.36✦ 18 The rest of the oil that is in the priest’s hand he shall put on the head of him who is to be cleansed, and the priest shall make atonement37 for him before Yahweh.3839✦ 19 “The priest shall offer the sin40 offering, and make atonement41 for him who is to be cleansed because of his uncleanness. Afterward he shall kill the burnt offering;✦ 20 then the priest shall offer the burnt offering and the meal offering on the altar. The priest shall make atonement42 for him, and he shall be clean.✦ 21 “If he is poor, and can’t afford so much, then he shall take one male lamb for a trespass offering to be waved, to make atonement43 for him, and one tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil for a meal offering, and a log of oil;44✦ 22 and two turtledoves, or two young pigeons, such as he is able to afford; and the one shall be a sin45 offering, and the other a burnt offering.46✦ 23 “On the eighth day he shall bring them for his cleansing to the priest, to the door of the Tent of Meeting, before Yahweh.47 24 The priest shall take the lamb of the trespass offering, and the log of oil, and the priest shall wave them for a wave offering before Yahweh.4849✦ 25 He shall kill the lamb of the trespass offering. The priest shall take some of the blood50 of the trespass offering and put it on the tip of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot.51✦ 26 The priest shall pour some of the oil into the palm of his own left hand; 27 and the priest shall sprinkle with his right finger some of the oil that is in his left hand seven times before Yahweh.52 28 Then the priest shall put some of the oil that is in his hand on the tip of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot, on the place of the blood53 of the trespass offering.54✦ 29 The rest of the oil that is in the priest’s hand he shall put on the head of him who is to be cleansed, to make atonement55 for him before Yahweh.5657 30 He shall offer one of the turtledoves, or of the young pigeons, which ever he is able to afford, 31 of the kind he is able to afford, the one for a sin58 offering, and the other for a burnt offering, with the meal offering. The priest shall make atonement59 for him who is to be cleansed before Yahweh.”60 32 This is the law for him in whom is the plague of leprosy, who is not able to afford the sacrifice for his cleansing. 33 Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying,61 34 “When you have come into the land62 of Canaan, which I give to you for a possession, and I put a spreading mildew in a house in the land of your possession,63✦ 35 then he who owns the house shall come and tell the priest, saying, ‘There seems to me to be some sort of plague in the house.’64✦ 36 The priest shall command that they empty65 the house, before the priest goes in to examine the plague, that all that is in the house not be made unclean. Afterward the priest shall go in to inspect the house.66✦ 37 He shall examine the plague; and behold, if the plague is in the walls of the house with hollow streaks, greenish or reddish, and it appears to be deeper than the wall,67✦ 38 then the priest shall go out of the house to the door of the house, and shut up the house seven days.68✦ 39 The priest shall come again on the seventh day, and look. If the plague has spread in the walls of the house,69✦ 40 then the priest shall command that they take out the stones in which is the plague, and cast them into an unclean place outside of the city.7071✦ 41 He shall cause the inside of the house to be scraped all over. They shall pour out the mortar that they scraped off outside of the city into an unclean place.7273✦ 42 They shall take other stones, and put them in the place of those stones; and he shall take other mortar, and shall plaster the house.74✦ 43 “If the plague comes again, and breaks out in the house after he has taken out the stones, and after he has scraped the house, and after it was plastered,75✦ 44 then the priest shall come in and look; and behold, if the plague has spread in the house, it is a destructive mildew in the house. It is unclean.76✦ 45 He shall break down the house, its stones, and its timber, and all the house’s mortar. He shall carry them out of the city into an unclean place.77✦ 46 “Moreover he who goes into the house while it is shut up shall be unclean until the evening.78✦ 47 He who lies down in the house shall wash his clothes; and he who eats in the house shall wash his clothes.79✦ 48 “If the priest shall come in, and examine it, and behold, the plague hasn’t spread in the house, after the house was plastered, then the priest shall pronounce the house clean, because the plague is healed.80✦ 49 To cleanse the house he shall take two birds, cedar wood, scarlet, and hyssop.81✦ 50 He shall kill one of the birds in an earthen vessel over running water82.83✦ 51 He shall take the cedar wood, the hyssop, the scarlet, and the living bird, and dip them in the blood84 of the slain bird, and in the running water85, and sprinkle the house seven times.86✦ 52 He shall cleanse the house with the blood87 of the bird, and with the running water88, with the living bird, with the cedar wood, with the hyssop, and with the scarlet;89✦ 53 but he shall let the living bird go out of the city into the open field. So shall he make atonement90 for the house; and it shall be clean.”91✦ 54 This is the law for any plague of leprosy, and for an itch,92 55 and for the destructive mildew of a garment, and for a house,93 56 and for a swelling, and for a scab, and for a bright spot;94 57 to teach when it is unclean, and when it is clean. This is the law of leprosy.95

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Vayyiqra (וַיִּקְרָא) — “and he called.” The Hebrew name of the book comes from this opening word. God calls Moses (a relational verb) before speaking to him; rabbinic tradition (Sifra) draws a contrast with Numbers 22, where God only speaks to Balaam — calling implies invitation. The English title Leviticus follows the LXX Leuitikon, “the Levitical [book],” though Levites as a class are barely mentioned in the book.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Olah (עֹלָה) — “that which goes up.” The most distinctive Israelite sacrifice: the entire animal, except the hide, is burnt on the altar — none is eaten. The name refers to the smoke ascending. Among ancient Near Eastern cultures the practice was unusual; most cultures fed sacrificial meat to the priests and worshippers. The whole-burnt offering signals total devotion — nothing is retained for human use. Distinct from the zevaḥ (peace offering, eaten communally) and the ḥattat (sin offering), the ‘olah is the most fully Godward sacrifice. The Greek LXX rendered it holokauston (“wholly burnt”), the source of the English word “holocaust.”

The same gesture later marks rabbinic ordination — the transfer of authority from teacher to student.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PAN a vessel of metal or earthenware used in culinary operations; a cooking-pan or frying-pan frequently referred to in the Old Testament (Leviticus 2:5; 6:21; Numbers 11:8; 1 Samuel 2:14, etc.). The “ash-pans” mentioned in Exodus 27:3 were made of copper, and were used in connection with the altar of burnt-offering. The “iron pan” mentioned in Ezekiel 4:3 (marg., “flat plate “ or “slice”) was probably a mere plate of iron used for baking. The “fire-pans” of Exodus 27:3 were fire-shovels used for taking up coals. The same Hebrew word is rendered “snuff-dishes” (25:38; 37:23) and “censers” (Leviticus 10:1; 16:12; Numbers 4:14, etc.). These were probably simply metal vessels employed for carrying burning embers from the brazen altar to the altar of incense. The “frying-pan” mentioned in Leviticus 2:7; 7:9 was a pot for boiling.

↩ ⌘ Word. Salt covenants in the ancient Near East. Salt was a near-universal symbol of inviolable agreement: it does not decay, it preserves, and a meal shared with salt was considered binding. Numbers 18:19 and 2 Chronicles 13:5 both use the phrase “covenant of salt” for unbreakable divine commitments. Arabic milḥah and the related notion of ‘aysh wa-milḥ (“bread and salt”) preserve the same custom.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Shelamim (שְׁלָמִים) — from the root shalom. Translated variously as “peace,” “fellowship,” or “well-being” offering. Unlike the burnt offering, the meat is shared between altar, priests, and worshippers — a celebratory communal meal in God’s presence. The root shalom covers wholeness, completeness, harmony; the offering is the only one regularly described as eaten in joy.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ABLUTION or washing, was practised, (1.) When a person was initiated into a higher state: e.g., when Aaron and his sons were set apart to the priest’s office, they were washed with water previous to their investiture with the priestly robes (Leviticus 8:6). (2.) Before the priests approached the altar of God, they were required, on pain of death, to wash their hands and their feet to cleanse them from the soil of common life (Exodus 30:17-21). To this practice the Psalmist alludes, Psalm 26:6. (3.) There were washings prescribed for the purpose of cleansing from positive defilement contracted by particular acts. Of such washings eleven different species are prescribed in the Levitical law (Leviticus 12-15). (4.) A fourth class of ablutions is mentioned, by which a person purified or absolved himself from the guilt of some particular act. For example, the elders of the nearest village where some murder was committed were required, when the murderer was unknown, to wash their hands over the expiatory heifer which was beheaded, and in doing so to say, “Our hands have not shed this blood, neither have our eyes seen it” (Deuteronomy 21:1-9). So also Pilate declared himself innocent of the blood of Jesus by washing his hands (Matthew 27:24). This act of Pilate may not, however, have been borrowed from the custom of the Jews. The same practice was common among the Greeks and Romans. The Pharisees carried the practice of ablution to great excess, thereby claiming extraordinary purity (Matthew 23:25). Mark (7:1-5) refers to the ceremonial ablutions. The Pharisees washed their hands “oft,” more correctly, “with the fist” (R.V., “diligently”), or as an old father, Theophylact, explains it, “up to the elbow.” (Compare also Mark 7:4; Leviticus 6:28; 11: 32-36; 15:22) (See WASHING.)

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Urim and Thummim (אוּרִים וְתֻמִּים) — “lights and perfections,” roughly. Sacred lots kept in the high priest’s breastplate, used to discern divine yes/no answers (1 Sam 14:41 LXX, 28:6, Num 27:21). Their physical form is never described — guesses include two stones, one black and one white; or inscribed dice. After the destruction of the first temple their use lapses; Ezra 2:63 anticipates a future priest who will restore them. They are the Bible’s clearest case of authorized ritual divination.

↩ ◇ Note. The death of Nadab and Abihu. The Hebrew esh zarah (“foreign fire”) is undefined — perhaps incense kindled from non-altar coals, perhaps a wrong recipe, perhaps an unauthorized timing. Multiple rabbinic readings (b. Sanhedrin 52a, Lev. Rabbah 20) blame various offences from drunkenness to spiritual ambition. The narrative leaves the offence deliberately under-specified; the lesson concerns the unmediated proximity of divine holiness, not the cataloguing of a particular sin.

↩ ◇ Note. The wine prohibition for serving priests. Linked by proximity to the death of Nadab and Abihu — many readers infer the brothers had been drinking. The prohibition applies only when entering the tent of meeting; it is not a general priestly abstention. The contrast with later Nazirite vows (Num 6) and the Rechabites (Jer 35) shows that the Hebrew Bible distinguishes ritual roles from total abstinence; the priesthood neither requires nor forbids wine in ordinary life.

↩ ◇ Note. The kosher logic. Mary Douglas’s influential anthropological reading (Purity and Danger, 1966) argues that animals classified as “clean” are those that perfectly match their domain — full hoof + full ruminant for land, fins + scales for water. Animals lacking either feature, or mixing categories (the pig has the hoof but lacks rumination), violate Israelite cosmic order. Other readings emphasize hygiene, ethical proximity to predators, or simple historical custom; Douglas’s structural reading is the dominant academic frame today.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Zevaḥ sh’lamim (זֶבַח שְׁלָמִים). The "peace offering" or "well-being offering" — the only sacrifice whose meat returned to the worshipper for a communal meal (7:15). Root shalom: completeness, peace, well-being. Unlike the wholly-burnt ‘olah, the sh’lamim created a shared table between God and worshipper, eaten in proximity to the sanctuary. Paul’s argument in 1 Cor 10:18 about "those who eat the sacrifices" being partners with the altar trades on this category.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Tzara‘at (צָרַעַת). Traditionally translated "leprosy," but the term covers a range of skin and surface conditions — including conditions of garments (13:47–59) and houses (14:33–53), which Hansen’s disease cannot affect. The framework is ritual-purity, not modern dermatology. The priest functions as a diagnostician of communal status, not as a physician. Naaman’s healing in 2 Kgs 5 and the Gospels’ leper-healings work within this framework, where the priest must certify the cleansing.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). LEVITICUS the third book of the Pentateuch; so called in the Vulgate, after the LXX., because it treats chiefly of the Levitical service. In the first section of the book (1-17), which exhibits the worship itself, there is, (1.) A series of laws (1-7) regarding sacrifices, burnt-offerings, meat-offerings, and thank-offerings (1-3), sin-offerings and trespass-offerings (4; 5), followed by the law of the priestly duties in connection with the offering of sacrifices (6; 7). (2.) An historical section (8-10), giving an account of the consecration of Aaron and his sons (8); Aaron’s first offering for himself and the people (9); Nadab and Abihu’s presumption in offering “strange fire before Jehovah,” and their punishment (10). (3.) Laws concerning purity, and the sacrifices and ordinances for putting away impurity (11-16). An interesting fact may be noted here. Canon Tristram, speaking of the remarkable discoveries regarding the flora and fauna of the Holy Land by the Palestine Exploration officers, makes the following statement:, “Take these two catalogues of the clean and unclean animals in the books of Leviticus [11] and Deuteronomy [14]. There are eleven in Deuteronomy which do not occur in Leviticus, and these are nearly all animals and birds which are not found in Egypt or the Holy Land, but which are numerous in the Arabian desert. They are not named in Leviticus a few weeks after the departure from Egypt; but after the people were thirty-nine years in the desert they are named, a strong proof that the list in Deuteronomy was written at the end of the journey, and the list in Leviticus at the beginning. It fixes the writing of that catalogue to one time and period only, viz., that when the children of Israel were familiar with the fauna and the flora of the desert” (Palest. Expl. Quart., Jan. 1887). (4.) Laws marking the separation between Israel and the heathen (17-20). (5.) Laws about the personal purity of the priests, and their eating of the holy things (20; 21); about the offerings of Israel, that they were to be without blemish (22:17-33); and about the due celebration of the great festivals (23; 25). (6.) Then follow promises and warnings to the people regarding obedience to these commandments, closing with a section on vows. The various ordinances contained in this book were all delivered in the space of a month (comp. Exodus 40:17; Numbers 1:1), the first month of the second year after the Exodus. It is the third book of Moses. No book contains more of the very words of God. He is almost throughout the whole of it the direct speaker. This book is a prophecy of things to come, a shadow whereof the substance is Christ and his kingdom. The principles on which it is to be interpreted are laid down in the Epistle to the Hebrews. It contains in its complicated ceremonial the gospel of the grace of God.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

When the tabernacle is finished, the cloud covers it and the glory of the Lord fills it. Ephrem reads the closing verse of Exodus as the canonical anticipation of the Apocalyptic vision: 'the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them' (Rev 21:3). The whole book moves from the house of bondage to the house of glory. Tewahedo eschatological catechesis treats Ex 40:34 as the OT bookend of the canonical hope completed in Rev 21.

↩ ◇ Note. The closing theophany. The book ends with the cloud filling the tabernacle so completely that even Moses cannot enter. The next book (Leviticus) opens with the call from inside that cloud — Moses now mediates by voice rather than sight. The transition: from Sinai (mountain), through Tabernacle (tent), eventually to Temple (house) — the trajectory of God’s indwelling presence among his people.

↩ ◇ Note. S’mikhah (סְמִיכָה). The hand-laying transfers identification — not sin (the offerer is not yet penitent), but ownership. The animal stands as a substitute self. The same gesture is used in ordination (Num 27:18, the ordaining of Joshua) and in ancient Jewish rabbinical authority transfer. Christian sacramental laying-on-of-hands draws from this tradition. Hebrews develops the substitution theology: an animal can foreshadow but not fulfill (Heb 10:4).

↩ ◇ Note. The high priest as representative. When the high priest sins, his sin endangers the whole people — "bringing guilt on the people" (4:3). The hierarchical structure of Leviticus assumes corporate identity: the priest represents the people Godward, and Israel represents the nations Godward. Failure at the top of this representational chain pollutes the whole. Hebrews 7:26–28 contrasts this with Christ: a high priest who does not need to sacrifice for his own sin first.

↩ ◇ Note. The death of Nadab and Abihu. The two priest-sons offer "strange fire" and are consumed. The narrative frames the disaster in cult-political terms: holiness is dangerous, and improvising at the altar is fatal. Aaron’s silence ("and Aaron held his peace") is one of the most poignant lines in the Pentateuch. Some midrashic traditions explore alcohol as the cause (preceded immediately by 10:9, the prohibition on drinking before service — perhaps placed there for that reason).

↩ ‖ Cite. Cross-references. Ezk 43:24.

↩ ◇ Note. Salt of the covenant. Salt as covenant-marker recurs in Num 18:19 ("a covenant of salt forever") and 2 Chr 13:5. Ancient Near Eastern parallels include shared meals sealed with salt as a sign of unbreakable bond — salt’s preservative quality stood in for permanence. Jesus in Mark 9:49–50 ("everyone will be salted with fire… have salt in yourselves") echoes the cultic-covenantal resonance, not just the table-seasoning sense.

↩ ◇ Note. The poor person’s offering. The chapter codifies a sliding-scale offering system: those who cannot afford a lamb may bring two birds; those who cannot afford even birds may bring a tenth of an ephah of fine flour (5:11). The provision is one of the OT’s clearest statements of cultic accommodation to economic reality — atonement is not gated by wealth, and the poorest Israelite has access to the same forgiveness as the wealthiest. Mary brings the two-bird offering after Jesus’ birth (Luke 2:24) — the explicit textual marker of the holy family’s poverty, and a deliberate Lukan signal connecting Jesus to the lowliest economic stratum of Israelite religious life. The verse is one of the OT roots of the principle, central to later prophetic and rabbinic ethics, that ritual obligations must be calibrated to capacity rather than imposed identically regardless of means.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). TRESPASS OFFERING (Hebrews ‘asham, “debt”), the law concerning, given in Leviticus 5:14-6:7; also in Numbers 5:5-8. The idea of sin as a “debt” pervades this legislation. The asham, which was always a ram, was offered in cases where sins were more private. (See OFFERING.)

↩ ◇ Note. The trespass offering. The asham ("trespass offering" or "guilt offering") covers a distinct category from the sin offering (chattat): unintentional violations of holy things — eating priestly food by mistake, withholding tithe by oversight, undervaluing a vow, etc. The offering required a ram of valuation plus a 20% restitution penalty (5:16) — the first OT articulation of restitution-plus-penalty as a moral-cultic principle. Isaiah 53:10 famously identifies the suffering servant’s soul as an asham, the first explicit OT use of the trespass-offering category for an interpretive theology of redemptive death. The chapter’s combination of restitution (returning what was taken plus penalty) with cultic atonement (the offering) creates a model — material amends plus spiritual reconciliation — that has shaped both Jewish penitential practice and Christian theology of repentance.

↩ ◇ Note. The perpetual fire. The chapter requires the altar fire — kindled originally by Yahweh himself (9:24, supernaturally) — to be maintained continuously, never extinguished. The provision encodes a theological principle: the human role is to preserve the divinely-given fire, not to generate it. Rabbinic tradition (m. Tamid 1:1) preserves elaborate procedures for the priestly night-watches that maintained the temple altar fire continuously through the Second Temple period. Christian liturgical tradition draws on the imagery: the perpetual sanctuary lamp before the Eucharistic reserve in Catholic and Orthodox churches descends conceptually from this verse, and Pentecostal theology of the "fire that does not go out" takes the chapter as paradigm. The verse is one of the OT’s clearest articulations of preservation-as-piety: religious fidelity is often less about generating new acts than refusing to let the originally-given gift die out.

↩ ◇ Note. The priests’ portion. The chapter specifies that the meat of the sin offering — except for the fat and the inwards burned on the altar — belongs to the priests. The provision is theologically dense: priests literally consume the sacrifice that bears the people’s sin, in the holy place, and in eating it they participate in the sin-bearing function of the cult. Hebrews 13:11–12 takes the verse as type for Christ’s suffering "outside the camp" (the sin offering whose body, in some specific cases, was burned outside the camp rather than eaten — Lev 4:11–12, 16:27 — distinguishing those grades of sin offering from the priest-eaten ones treated here). The arrangement combines economic provision (priests eat from offerings) with theological symbolism (priests bear sin by ingestion) in characteristic Levitical fashion, making the priestly office both materially supported and ritually freighted in the same act.

↩ ◇ Note. The order of atonement. Moses’ instruction to Aaron at the inaugural sacrifice — atone for yourself first, then for the people — encodes a principle that runs through the entire OT and NT priesthood theology: the priest must be cleansed before he can mediate cleansing for others. The same principle drives the Day of Atonement procedure (Lev 16:6, 11), where Aaron sacrifices a bull for himself and his household before offering the goats for Israel. Hebrews 7:27 cites this exact sequence to argue Christ’s priestly superiority — unlike Aaron, Christ "had no need to offer up sacrifices first for his own sins, then for those of the people." The verse is the textual root of the Christological argument that the priest’s sinlessness is what makes the priestly sacrifice non-repeatable: where Aaron’s priestly cleansing requires daily renewal, Christ’s sinlessness allows once-for-all sacrifice. The OT pattern remains theological pre-condition for the NT argument.

↩ ◇ Note. The divine ignition. Yahweh himself kindles the inaugural altar fire — the same theophanic pattern that consumes Elijah’s offering on Carmel (1 Kgs 18:38) and David’s sacrifice at Araunah’s threshing floor (1 Chr 21:26), and that descends as Pentecostal flames in Acts 2:3. The pattern across these passages is consistent: the legitimate sanctuary is one where the fire comes from above, not from below. The Christian Pentecost narrative (Acts 2) draws explicitly on this OT pattern: the tongues of fire descending on the apostles inaugurate the church’s priestly-Spirit-bearing function in the same way Yahweh’s descended fire inaugurated the priestly cult here. The verse establishes a recurrent OT-NT theological motif: divine institution validates a worship-space by visible fire from heaven. The chapter’s placement (the inaugural sacrifice immediately preceding the Nadab-and-Abihu disaster of Lev 10) sets up the contrast between divinely-given fire (legitimate) and "strange fire" (deadly).

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: ANIMALS, FOOD, GOAT, SANITATION.

↩ ◇ Note. Kashrut criteria. The land-animal criterion is twofold: cloven-hoofed AND chewing the cud. Possible explanations have multiplied — hygienic (Maimonides), symbolic-categorical (Mary Douglas, Purity and Danger: holiness = wholeness within categories), economic (favoring herd animals), and theological (visible markers of Israelite distinctiveness). Douglas’s reading remains influential: the dietary rules instantiate a vision of divine order in which every creature belongs to a clean category, and anomalies (pig: cloven hoof but no cud; camel: cud but no proper cloven hoof) are excluded.

↩ ◇ Note. The post-childbirth offering. The chapter requires a postpartum mother to bring a year-old lamb plus a turtledove or pigeon at the end of her purification period — forty days for a son, eighty for a daughter (12:4–5). The lamb is the burnt offering (worship-restoration); the bird is the sin offering (purification). The provision is the cultic context of Mary’s presentation in Luke 2:22–24, where she brings the poor person’s alternative (two birds) — the same chapter’s sliding-scale provision in Lev 12:8. The asymmetric purification periods (forty vs. eighty days for sons vs. daughters) are unexplained in the text and have generated centuries of speculation; modern feminist scholarship has read them as encoding patriarchal devaluation, while others read them as protective accommodation (longer rest period for the mother of a daughter who will eventually menstruate). The chapter’s blunt biological focus — bodily fluids, female purity, ritual impurity surrounding birth — reflects the OT’s general assumption that human biology is intrinsically connected to cultic status.

↩ ◇ Note. Mary’s offering. The verse provides the explicit textual ground for the New Testament’s claim that the Holy Family was poor: Luke 2:24 records Mary bringing exactly this offering — "a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons" — at Jesus’ presentation in the temple. Luke’s readers steeped in Septuagint Greek would have recognized the precise verbal echo of Lev 12:8. The detail is not incidental — Luke is building a sustained Christological argument about Jesus’ identification with the poor, and the choice of offering at Mary’s purification is the first concrete economic marker. Combined with the manger setting, the absence of a household for the visiting magi (Matt 2:11 a "house," but only after travel), and Joseph’s carpenter trade, the Lukan portrait is consistent. The verse is one of the OT’s small specific texts that becomes load-bearing in NT Christological reflection on the social location of the incarnation.

↩ ◇ Note. The cleansing-from-leprosy ritual. The chapter’s elaborate purification rite for the recovered "leper" (the Hebrew tzara‘at covers a range of skin conditions, not modern Hansen’s disease) involves two birds, cedar wood, scarlet thread, and hyssop — the same four cultic substances as the red-heifer ash ritual in Num 19. One bird is killed over running water; the other is dipped in the blood and released alive into the open field. The pattern — one death, one release, both required for purification — has been read typologically by Christian commentators (Augustine, Origen) as anticipating the death-and-resurrection of Christ. Beyond the typological reading, the ritual also functions sociologically: the released bird carries the impurity outward into uninhabited space, a scapegoat-style expulsion paralleling the Yom Kippur goat sent to Azazel (Lev 16:21–22). The chapter is one of the OT’s most procedurally elaborate rituals and one of its most theologically suggestive.

↩ ◇ Note. The seven sprinklings. The number seven recurs throughout the cleansing ritual — seven sprinklings of blood (here), seven days outside the tent (14:8), seven-day waiting period before re-examination — and across Levitical purification more broadly. Seven in OT cultic numerology signals completeness, divine order, and full repetition; the seven-fold sprinkling is not just abundant but theologically definitive. The same numerological pattern recurs in Christian sacramental practice: the threefold-trine (rather than seven-fold) baptismal pouring in early church practice, the seven sacraments of medieval Catholic theology, the seven words from the cross. The verse establishes one of the OT’s most-imitated ritual numerical patterns. Practically, the seven days outside the camp provided medical observation time — the same condition could clear up over a week — making the ritual function partially as ancient infectious-disease management combined with cultic restoration.

↩ ◇ Note. The blood-and-fat prohibition. Two perpetual statutes are paired in this verse: no eating of fat (the energy-rich tissue surrounding internal organs, reserved for the altar), and no eating of blood (the carrier of life, reserved for atonement). The blood prohibition extends well beyond the cultic context — Gen 9:4 places it in the Noahide covenant, before any Israelite-specific legislation, making it one of the OT’s few universal moral provisions. Acts 15:20, 29 carries it forward into the apostolic decree as one of the four obligations placed on Gentile Christians. The fat prohibition is more narrowly cultic and effectively lapses with the temple, but the blood prohibition runs through all subsequent Jewish dietary law and shaped the Christian theology of Christ’s blood as uniquely redemptive (Heb 9:22, "without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness"). The verse is the textual root of a chain of biblical-theological reflection on blood that spans the entire canon.

↩ ◇ Note. Corporate guilt. The chapter recognizes a category modern legal thought has largely abandoned: the unintentional sin of an entire community as a culpable category requiring atonement. The provision encodes the OT’s commitment to corporate moral identity — Israel sins and atones as a body, not just as individuals. The same theology drives the Day of Atonement procedure (Lev 16), Achan’s sin compromising all Israel at Ai (Josh 7), and the prophetic confessions of national guilt (Jer 14, Dan 9, Neh 9) where Israel’s representatives confess sins they themselves did not commit. Corporate-confessional liturgy in modern Catholic and Reformed traditions (the Confiteor, the prayer of confession) descends from this OT pattern. The Hebrew Bible operates with a thicker conception of corporate identity than modern individualism easily accommodates, and this chapter is one of its clearer demonstrations.

↩ ◇ Note. The wave offering. The tenufah ("wave offering") involved literally lifting the offering and moving it horizontally — a ritual gesture distinguishing the offering as Yahweh’s portion before it was distributed to the priests. The motion-symbolism is theological: visible elevation marks the transfer of property from worshipper to deity, then back from deity to priestly portion. The wave offering covered specific portions (typically the breast) of peace offerings, and its priestly recipients (the breast went to the officiating priest, the right thigh as a "heave offering" went to the high priest, 7:33–34) created a structured economic provision for the priesthood from each peace offering brought by ordinary Israelites. The gesture has had liturgical afterlife in Christian elevation of the host during the Eucharist — visible elevation marking transfer from common to sacred, then return for distribution.

↩ ◇ Note. The ordination blood. The blood-application to ear, thumb, and big toe encodes a ritual logic: the senses through which divine revelation enters (the ear that hears Yahweh’s word), the agency that performs cultic work (the hand that handles holy things), and the mobility that approaches the sanctuary (the foot that walks in holy spaces) — all three are consecrated by blood. The same triad appears at 14:14 in the cleansing of the leper, suggesting the ear-thumb-toe pattern is a general consecration formula for priestly-grade access to holiness. Christian sacramental tradition picks up the pattern: the anointing of senses in some baptismal rites, the consecration of hands in priestly ordination. The verse is one of the OT’s most concretely embodied ritual gestures — sanctification that does not merely declare or symbolize, but physically marks the parts of the body involved in the sacred work.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HARE (Hebrews ‘arnebeth) was prohibited as food according to the Mosaic law (Leviticus 11:6; Deuteronomy 14:7), “because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof.” The habit of this animal is to grind its teeth and move its jaw as if it actually chewed the cud. But, like the cony (q.v.), it is not a ruminant with four stomachs, but a rodent like the squirrel, rat, etc. Moses speaks of it according to appearance. It is interdicted because, though apparently chewing the cud, it did not divide the hoof. There are two species in Syria, (1) the Lepus Syriacus or Syrian hare, which is like the English hare; and (2) the Lepus Sinaiticus, or hare of the desert. No rabbits are found in Syria.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SWINE (Hebrews hazir), regarded as the most unclean and the most abhorred of all animals (Leviticus 11:7; Isaiah 65:4; 66:3, 17; Luke 15:15, 16). A herd of swine were drowned in the Sea of Galilee (Luke 8:32, 33). Spoken of figuratively in Matthew 7:6 (see Proverbs 11:22). It is frequently mentioned as a wild animal, and is evidently the wild boar (Arab. khanzir), which is common among the marshes of the Jordan valley (Psalm 80:13).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). OSPREY Hebrews ‘ozniyyah, an unclean bird according to the Mosaic law (Leviticus 11:13; Deuteronomy 14:12); the fish-eating eagle (Pandion haliaetus); one of the lesser eagles. But the Hebrew word may be taken to denote the short-toed eagle (Circaetus gallicus of Southern Europe), one of the most abundant of the eagle tribe found in Palestine.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). OSSIFRAGE Hebrews peres = to “break” or “crush”, the lammer-geier, or bearded vulture, the largest of the whole vulture tribe. It was an unclean bird (Leviticus 11:13; Deuteronomy 14:12). It is not a gregarious bird, and is found but rarely in Palestine. “When the other vultures have picked the flesh off any animal, he comes in at the end of the feast, and swallows the bones, or breaks them, and swallows the pieces if he cannot otherwise extract the marrow. The bones he cracks [hence the appropriateness of the name ossifrage, i.e., “bone-breaker”] by letting them fall on a rock from a great height. He does not, however, confine himself to these delicacies, but whenever he has an opportunity will devour lambs, kids, or hares. These he generally obtains by pushing them over cliffs, when he has watched his opportunity; and he has been known to attack men while climbing rocks, and dash them against the bottom. But tortoises and serpents are his ordinary food...No doubt it was a lammer-geier that mistook the bald head of the poet AEschylus for a stone, and dropped on it the tortoise which killed him” (Tristram’s Nat. Hist.).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). KITE an unclean and keen-sighted bird of prey (Leviticus 11:14; Deuteronomy 14:13). The Hebrew word used, ’ayet, is rendered “vulture” in Job 28:7 in Authorized Version, “falcon” in Revised Version. It is probably the red kite (Milvus regalis), a bird of piercing sight and of soaring habits found all over Palestine.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). VULTURE (1.) Hebrews da’ah (Leviticus 11:14). In the parallel passage (Deuteronomy 14:13) the Hebrew word used is ra’ah, rendered “glede;” LXX., “gups;” Vulg., “milvus.” A species of ravenous bird, distinguished for its rapid flight. “When used without the epithet ‘red,’ the name is commonly confined to the black kite. The habits of the bird bear out the allusion in Isaiah 34:15, for it is, excepting during the winter three months, so numerous everywhere in Palestine as to be almost gregarious.” (See EAGLE.) (2.) In Job 28:7 the Hebrews ‘ayyah is thus rendered. The word denotes a clamorous and a keen-sighted bird of prey. In Leviticus 11:14 and Deuteronomy 14:13 it is rendered “kite” (q.v.). W

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: BIRDS, CUCKOO, FOOD, HAWK, NIGHT HAWK.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CUCKOO (Hebrews shahaph), from a root meaning “to be lean; slender.” This bird is mentioned only in Leviticus 11:16 and Deuteronomy 14:15 (R.V., “seamew”). Some have interpreted the Hebrew word by “petrel” or “shearwater” (Puffinus cinereus), which is found on the coast of Syria; others think it denotes the “sea-gull” or “seamew.” The common cuckoo (Cuculus canorus) feeds on reptiles and large insects. It is found in Asia and Africa as well as in Europe. It only passes the winter in Palestine. The Arabs suppose it to utter the cry Yakub, and hence they call it tir el-Yakub; i.e., “Jacob’s bird.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HAWK (Hebrews netz, a word expressive of strong and rapid flight, and hence appropriate to the hawk). It is an unclean bird (Leviticus 11:16; Deuteronomy 14:15). It is common in Syria and surrounding countries. The Hebrew word includes various species of Falconidae, with special reference perhaps to the kestrel (Falco tinnunculus), the hobby (Hypotriorchis subbuteo), and the lesser kestrel (Tin, Cenchris). The kestrel remains all the year in Palestine, but some ten or twelve other species are all migrants from the south. Of those summer visitors to Palestine special mention may be made of the Falco sacer and the Falco lanarius. (See NIGHT-HAWK.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). NIGHT-HAWK (Hebrews tahmas) occurs only in the list of unclean birds (Leviticus 11:16; Deuteronomy 14:15). This was supposed to be the night-jar (Caprimulgus), allied to the swifts. The Hebrew word is derived from a root meaning “to scratch or tear the face,” and may be best rendered, in accordance with the ancient versions, “an owl” (Strix flammea). The Revised Version renders “night-hawk.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). OWL (1.) Hebrews bath-haya’anah, “daughter of greediness” or of “shouting.” In the list of unclean birds (Leviticus 11:16; Deuteronomy 14:15); also mentioned in Job 30:29; Isaiah 13:21; 34:13; 43:20; Jeremiah 50:39; Micah 1:8. In all these passages the Revised Version translates “ostrich” (q.v.), which is the correct rendering. (2.) Hebrews yanshuph, rendered “great owl” in Leviticus 11:17; Deuteronomy 14:16, and “owl” in Isaiah 34:11. This is supposed to be the Egyptian eagle-owl (Bubo ascalaphus), which takes the place of the eagle-owl (Bubo maximus) found in Southern Europe. It is found frequenting the ruins of Egypt and also of the Holy Land. “Its cry is a loud, prolonged, and very powerful hoot. I know nothing which more vividly brought to my mind the sense of desolation and loneliness than the re-echoing hoot of two or three of these great owls as I stood at midnight among the ruined temples of Baalbek” (Tristram). The LXX. and Vulgate render this word by “ibis”, i.e., the Egyptian heron. (3.) Hebrews kos, rendered “little owl” in Leviticus 11:17; Deuteronomy 14:16, and “owl” in Psalm 102:6. The Arabs call this bird “the mother of ruins.” It is by far the most common of all the owls of Palestine. It is the Athene persica, the bird of Minerva, the symbol of ancient Athens. (4.) Hebrews kippoz, the “great owl” (Isaiah 34:15); Revised Version, “arrow-snake;” LXX. and Vulgate, “hedgehog,” reading in the text, kippod, instead of kippoz. There is no reason to doubt the correctness of the rendering of the Authorized Version. Tristram says: “The word [i.e., kippoz] is very possibly an imitation of the cry of the scops owl (Scops giu), which is very common among ruins, caves, and old walls of towns...It is a migrant, returning to Palestine in spring.” (5.) Hebrews lilith, “screech owl” (Isaiah 34:14, marg. and R.V., “night monster”). The Hebrew word is from a root signifying “night.” Some species of the owl is obviously intended by this word. It may be the hooting or tawny owl (Syrnium aluco), which is common in Egypt and in many parts of Palestine. This verse in Isaiah is “descriptive of utter and perpetual desolation, of a land that should be full of ruins, and inhabited by the animals that usually make such ruins their abode.”

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: BIRDS, CORMORANT, FOOD, OWL, SANITATION.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CORMORANT (Leviticus 11:17; Deuteronomy 14:17), Hebrews shalak, “plunging,” or “darting down,” (the Phalacrocorax carbo), ranked among the “unclean” birds; of the same family group as the pelican. It is a “plunging” bird, and is common on the coasts and the island seas of Palestine. Some think the Hebrew word should be rendered “gannet” (Sula bassana, “the solan goose”); others that it is the “tern” or “sea swallow,” which also frequents the coasts of Palestine as well as the Sea of Galilee and the Jordan valley during several months of the year. But there is no reason to depart from the ordinary rendering. In Isaiah 34:11, Zephaniah 2:14 (but in R.V., “pelican”) the Hebrew word rendered by this name is ka’ath. It is translated “pelican” (q.v.) in Psalm 102:6. The word literally means the “vomiter,” and the pelican is so called from its vomiting the shells and other things which it has voraciously swallowed. (See PELICAN.)

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Birds, Birds, Birds, Birds, Birds.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: BIRDS, EAGLE, FOOD, PELICAN, SANITATION.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GIER EAGLE Hebrews raham = “parental affection,” Leviticus 11:18; Deuteronomy 14:17; R.V., “vulture”), a species of vulture living entirely on carrion. “It is about the size of a raven; has an almost triangular, bald, and wrinkled head, a strong pointed beak, black at the tip, large eyes and ears, the latter entirely on the outside, and long feet.” It is common in Egypt, where it is popularly called “Pharaoh’s chicken” (the Neophron percnopterus), and is found in Palestine only during summer. Tristram thinks that the Hebrew name, which is derived from a root meaning “to love,” is given to it from the fact that the male and female bird never part company.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PELICANS are frequently met with at the waters of Merom and the Sea of Galilee. The pelican is ranked among unclean birds (Leviticus 11:18; Deuteronomy 14:17). It is of an enormous size, being about 6 feet long, with wings stretching out over 12 feet. The Hebrew name (kaath, i.e., “vomiter”) of this bird is incorrectly rendered “cormorant” in the Authorized Version of Isaiah 34:11 and Zephaniah 2:14, but correctly in the Revised Version. It receives its Hebrew name from its habit of storing in its pouch large quantities of fish, which it disgorges when it feeds its young. Two species are found on the Syrian coast, the Pelicanus onocrotalus, or white pelican, and the Pelicanus crispus, or Dalmatian pelican.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SWAN mentioned in the list of unclean birds (Leviticus 11:18; Deuteronomy 14:16), is sometimes met with in the Jordan and the Sea of Galilee.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Birds, Birds, Birds, Denunciations against.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: BAT, BIRDS, FOOD, HERON, LAPWING.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BAT The Hebrew word (atalleph’) so rendered (Leviticus 11:19; Deuteronomy 14:18) implies “flying in the dark.” The bat is reckoned among the birds in the list of unclean animals. To cast idols to the “moles and to the bats” means to carry them into dark caverns or desolate places to which these animals resort (Isaiah 2:20), i.e., to consign them to desolation or ruin.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HERON (Leviticus 11:19; Deuteronomy 14:18), ranked among the unclean birds. The Hebrew name is ’anaphah, and indicates that the bird so named is remarkable for its angry disposition. “The herons are wading-birds, peculiarly irritable, remarkable for their voracity, frequenting marshes and oozy rivers, and spread over the regions of the East.” The Ardea russeta, or little golden egret, is the commonest species in Asia.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). LAPWING the name of an unclean bird, mentioned only in Leviticus 11:19 and Deuteronomy 14:18. The Hebrew name of this bird, dukiphath, has been generally regarded as denoting the hoope (Upupa epops), an onomatopoetic word derived from the cry of the bird, which resembles the word “hoop;” a bird not uncommon in Palestine. Others identify it with the English peewit.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). STORK Hebrews hasidah, meaning “kindness,” indicating thus the character of the bird, which is noted for its affection for its young. It is in the list of birds forbidden to be eaten by the Levitical law (Leviticus 11:19; Deuteronomy 14:18). It is like the crane, but larger in size. Two species are found in Palestine, the white, which are dispersed in pairs over the whole country; and the black, which live in marshy places and in great flocks. They migrate to Palestine periodically (about the 22nd of March). Jeremiah alludes to this (Jeremiah 8:7). At the appointed time they return with unerring sagacity to their old haunts, and re-occupy their old nests. “There is a well-authenticated account of the devotion of a stork which, at the burning of the town of Delft, after repeated and unsuccessful attempts to carry off her young, chose rather to remain and perish with them than leave them to their fate. Well might the Romans call it the pia avis!” In Job 39:13 (A.V.), instead of the expression “or wings and feathers unto the ostrich” (marg., “the feathers of the stork and ostrich”), the Revised Version has “are her pinions and feathers kindly” (marg., instead of “kindly,” reads “like the stork’s”). The object of this somewhat obscure verse seems to be to point out a contrast between the stork, as distinguished for her affection for her young, and the ostrich, as distinguished for her indifference. Zechariah (5:9) alludes to the beauty and power of the stork’s wings.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BEETLE (Hebrews hargol, meaning “leaper”). Mention of it is made only in Leviticus 11:22, where it is obvious the word cannot mean properly the beetle. It denotes some winged creeper with at least four feet, “which has legs above its feet, to leap withal.” The description plainly points to the locust (q.v.). This has been an article of food from the earliest times in the East to the present day. The word is rendered “cricket” in the Revised Version.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). TORTOISE (Hebrews tsabh). Ranked among the unclean animals (Leviticus 11:29). Land tortoises are common in Syria. The LXX. renders the word by “land crocodile.” The word, however, more probably denotes a lizard, called by the modern Arabs dhabb.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). WEASEL (Hebrews holedh), enumerated among unclean animals (Leviticus 11:29). Some think that this Hebrew word rather denotes the mole (Spalax typhlus) common in Palestine. There is no sufficient reason, however, to depart from the usual translation. The weasel tribe are common also in Palestine.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Beard, The, Beard, The, Reptiles.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: CHAMELEON, CREEPING THINGS, CREEPING THINGS, FERRET, FOOD.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CHAMELEON a species of lizard which has the faculty of changing the colour of its skin. It is ranked among the unclean animals in Leviticus 11:30, where the Hebrew word so translated is coah (R.V., “land crocodile”). In the same verse the Hebrew tanshemeth, rendered in Authorized Version “mole,” is in Revised Version “chameleon,” which is the correct rendering. This animal is very common in Egypt and in the Holy Land, especially in the Jordan valley.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). FERRET Leviticus 11:30 (R.V., “gecko”), one of the unclean creeping things. It was perhaps the Lacerta gecko which was intended by the Hebrew word (anakah, a cry, “mourning,” the creature which groans) here used, i.e., the “fan-footed” lizard, the gecko which makes a mournful wail. The LXX. translate it by a word meaning “shrew-mouse,” of which there are three species in Palestine. The Rabbinical writers regard it as the hedgehog. The translation of the Revised Version is to be preferred.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). LIZARD Only in Leviticus 11:30, as rendering of Hebrew letaah, so called from its “hiding.” Supposed to be the Lacerta gecko or fan-foot lizard, from the toes of which poison exudes. (See CHAMELEON.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MOLE Hebrews tinshameth (Leviticus 11:30), probably signifies some species of lizard (rendered in R.V., “chameleon”). In Leviticus 11:18, Deuteronomy 14:16, it is rendered, in Authorized Version, “swan” (R.V., “horned owl”). The Hebrews holed (Leviticus 11:29), rendered “weasel,” was probably the mole-rat. The true mole (Talpa Europoea) is not found in Palestine. The mole-rat (Spalax typhlus) “is twice the size of our mole, with no external eyes, and with only faint traces within of the rudimentary organ; no apparent ears, but, like the mole, with great internal organs of hearing; a strong, bare snout, and with large gnawing teeth; its colour a pale slate; its feet short, and provided with strong nails; its tail only rudimentary.” In Isaiah 2:20, this word is the rendering of two words haphar peroth, which are rendered by Gesenius “into the digging of rats”, i.e., rats’ holes. But these two Hebrew words ought probably to be combined into one (lahporperoth) and translated “to the moles”, i.e., the rat-moles. This animal “lives in underground communities, making large subterranean chambers for its young and for storehouses, with many runs connected with them, and is decidedly partial to the loose debris among ruins and stone-heaps, where it can form its chambers with least trouble.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SNAIL (1.) Hebrews homit, among the unclean creeping things (Leviticus 11:30). This was probably the sand-lizard, of which there are many species in the wilderness of Judea and the Sinai peninsula. (2.) Hebrews shablul (Psalm 58:8), the snail or slug proper. Tristram explains the allusions of this passage by a reference to the heat and drought by which the moisture of the snail is evaporated. “We find,” he says, “in all parts of the Holy Land myriads of snail-shells in fissures still adhering by the calcareous exudation round their orifice to the surface of the rock, but the animal of which is utterly shrivelled and wasted, ‘melted away.’”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). RANGES (1.) Leviticus 11:35. Probably a cooking furnace for two or more pots, as the Hebrew word here is in the dual number; or perhaps a fire-place fitted to receive a pair of ovens. (2.) 2 Kings 11:8. A Hebrew word is here used different from the preceding, meaning “ranks of soldiers.” The Levites were appointed to guard the king’s person within the temple (2 Chronicles 23:7), while the soldiers were his guard in the court, and in going from the temple to the palace. The soldiers are here commanded to slay any one who should break through the “ranks” (as rendered in the R.V.) to come near the king. In 2 Kings 11:15 the expression, “Have her forth without the ranges,” is in the Revised Version, “Have her forth between the ranks;” i.e., Jehoiada orders that Athaliah should be kept surrounded by his own guards, and at the same time conveyed beyond the precincts of the temple.

↩ ◇ Note. The holiness imperative. The verse is one of the OT’s most theologically concentrated formulations: human holiness is grounded in and modeled on divine holiness. The same formula recurs at Lev 19:2, 20:7, 20:26, 21:8 — anchoring the so-called "Holiness Code" (Lev 17–26) — and is taken up in 1 Pet 1:16 ("be holy, for I am holy") as the Christian appropriation. The Hebrew qadosh ("holy") fundamentally means "set apart, separated for divine purpose"; the imperative does not require moral perfection in the abstract but a corresponding distinctness of life that mirrors Yahweh’s own otherness. The chapter’s placement of the holiness imperative immediately after the dietary laws is theologically deliberate: the most ordinary acts (eating) are the daily pedagogy in covenantal distinctness. Few OT verses have so durable a moral-theological afterlife.

↩ ◇ Note. The leper’s lament. The chapter requires the diagnosed "leper" (the OT category includes various skin conditions, not just modern Hansen’s disease) to wear torn clothes, leave hair disheveled, cover the upper lip, and cry "Unclean! Unclean!" while approaching anyone. The triple marker — visual (torn clothes, loose hair), physical (covered lip), vocal (cry of warning) — overdetermines the social isolation. The provision sits awkwardly in modern reading: it produces real human suffering (forced isolation, public shame) for a condition the sufferer did not cause. The OT itself records the cost — Naaman’s desperation (2 Kgs 5), Miriam’s seven-day exile (Num 12), Uzziah’s isolation (2 Chr 26:21), the ten lepers Jesus heals (Luke 17:11–19) all keeping the legal distance the verse requires. Jesus’ deliberate touching of lepers (Mark 1:41) reads against this background as a calculated reversal of the chapter’s required separation. The verse is the textual root of one of the OT’s most socially difficult institutions.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Peace Offerings.

↩ ◇ Note. The priestly portions. Two specific cuts of every peace-offering — the breast (waved before Yahweh in a horizontal motion) and the right thigh (heaved upward) — are reserved as the priesthood’s permanent share. The motions are not merely decorative; they ritually mark the cuts as being given to Yahweh and then returned to the priests as proxies. The same procedure underwrites the priesthood’s economic livelihood: priests do not own land (cf. Num 18:20) but eat regularly from offerings, with these specific cuts forming the predictable share. The verse is institutionally important — it specifies how a non-landed religious class is sustained inside an agrarian economy, by sacralizing a fraction of every meat-offering brought to the sanctuary. The arrangement keeps priestly economic interests aligned with the offering system itself: the priesthood prospers when the offerings flow, suffers when they stop.

↩ ◇ Note. The ordination ram. The chapter narrates the seven-day ordination ceremony of Aaron and his sons (cf. Exod 29 for the prescription). The "ram of consecration" — Hebrew eil ha-millu’im, literally "ram of fillings" or "ram of installation" — is the central offering: its blood is applied to the right ear, right thumb, and right big toe of each priest (8:23–24), consecrating ear (to hear Yahweh’s instruction), hand (to perform sanctuary work), and foot (to walk the holy precincts). The same procedure recurs at 14:14 in the leper’s purification ritual — the cleansed leper is "re-ordained" into normal Israelite life by exactly the priestly ordination procedure. The parallel is theologically significant: the procedure that creates a priest also restores an outcast to community membership. Lev 8 supplies the textual basis for nearly all later Christian ordination liturgy (laying on of hands, anointing, vesting, sevenfold structure), descending through Hippolytus’s Apostolic Tradition to medieval and modern rites.

↩ ◇ Note. The glory-cloud arrives. The book’s closing scene: as soon as Moses finishes assembling the tabernacle, the cloud of Yahweh’s presence covers it and the divine glory (Hebrew kavod) fills the structure so densely that even Moses cannot enter. The image is of theological completion — the engineered meeting-place actually receives the deity it was designed to host. The same cloud-and-glory will later fill Solomon’s temple (1 Kgs 8:10–11) at the dedication, with the same effect (the priests cannot enter); will depart in Ezekiel’s vision (Ezek 10–11) at the temple’s defilement; and will return in Ezekiel’s eschatological temple (Ezek 43:1–5). The cloud thus traces the entire OT theology of divine presence with sanctuary across the canon. John 1:14 ("the Word became flesh and tabernacled [eskēnōsen] among us, and we beheld his glory") deliberately echoes this verse, claiming the incarnate Christ as the new tabernacle in which God’s glory dwells. The book of Exodus, which began with Israel groaning under Egyptian oppression (1:11), ends with Yahweh’s glory dwelling in their midst. The narrative arc is theologically complete.

↩ ◇ Note. The salt covenant. Salt — preservative, antiseptic, indispensable — becomes one of the OT’s most distinctive covenant-symbols precisely because it does not spoil. The phrase b’rit melaḥ ("covenant of salt") recurs at Num 18:19 (the priestly portion) and 2 Chr 13:5 (the Davidic kingship), framing those covenants as permanent because indestructible. Salt’s practical role in ANE treaty-meals — shared salt sealed agreements, a custom preserved in Arabic milḥa idioms for loyalty bonds — underwrites the symbolism: covenant-partners "share salt" with Yahweh in every cereal offering. Jesus’ "you are the salt of the earth" (Matt 5:13) draws on this OT covenant-imagery, with the seasoning function presupposing the preservation function. The verse is one of the OT’s small but theologically dense provisions, with semantic afterlife well beyond Leviticus.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Church of Israel, Offerings, Sacrifices, Sin Offering.

↩ ◇ Note. The communal sin offering. The chapter establishes a hierarchy of sin offerings calibrated to the offender: a high priest sins (4:3), the whole congregation sins (4:13), a leader sins (4:22), an individual commoner sins (4:27). The graded offerings — bull for the priest and the congregation, male goat for the leader, female goat or lamb for the commoner — match the social weight of the sinner: greater status produces greater liability. The principle that the community as a corporate body can sin and require atonement is one of the OT’s most important departures from purely individualist moral frameworks. The Day of Atonement liturgy (ch 16) operates this principle at maximum: an entire year of communal infractions is purged through one elaborate ritual sequence. Christian theological tradition takes this corporate-sin framework seriously as background to ecclesiology — the church as a body that can collectively sin and require communal repentance, not just an aggregate of individual sinners.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Head, Leprosy, Leprosy, Pride, Sickness.

↩ ◇ Note. The leper’s self-warning. The verse codifies one of the OT’s most poignant requirements: the person diagnosed with tzara‘at (the broad category encompassing what English calls "leprosy" but covering many skin conditions and even mildew on garments and houses) must walk through the community calling out his own ritual status. The provision combines several functions: practical (warning others to avoid contagion of impurity), ritual (the sufferer publicly performs his own classification), and pastoral (the verse seems to implicitly recognize the sufferer’s grief, with the torn clothes and uncovered head being standard mourning gestures, which the provision makes mandatory for the leper). Jesus’ healing of the ten lepers in Luke 17:11–19 picks up the verse’s structure deliberately — they "stood at a distance" and "lifted up their voices," obeying this exact provision; their cry of "have mercy on us" replaces the cry of "Unclean! Unclean!" The Christian interpretive tradition often treats the lepers’ reframed cry as the moment Jesus’ presence reorients the entire Levitical purity logic.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BIRD Birds are divided in the Mosaic law into two classes, (1) the clean (Leviticus 1:14-17; 5:7-10; 14:4-7), which were offered in sacrifice; and (2) the unclean (Leviticus 11:13-20). When offered in sacrifice, they were not divided as other victims were (Genesis 15:10). They are mentioned also as an article of food (Deuteronomy 14:11). The art of snaring wild birds is referred to (Psalm 124:7; Proverbs 1:17; 7:23; Jeremiah 5:27). Singing birds are mentioned in Psalm 104:12; Ecclesiastes 12:4. Their timidity is alluded to (Hos. 11:11). The reference in Psalm 84:3 to the swallow and the sparrow may be only a comparison equivalent to, “What her house is to the sparrow, and her nest to the swallow, that thine altars are to my soul.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SATYR hairy one. Mentioned in Greek mythology as a creature composed of a man and a goat, supposed to inhabit wild and desolate regions. The Hebrew word is rendered also “goat” (Leviticus 4:24) and “devil”, i.e., an idol in the form of a goat (17:7; 2 Chronicles 11:15). When it is said (Isaiah 13:21; comp. 34:14) “the satyrs shall dance there,” the meaning is that the place referred to shall become a desolate waste. Some render the Hebrew word “baboon,” a species of which is found in Babylonia.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). WOOL one of the first material used for making woven cloth (Leviticus 13:47, 48, 52, 59; 19:19). The first-fruit of wool was to be offered to the priests (Deuteronomy 18:4). The law prohibiting the wearing of a garment “of divers sorts, as of woollen and linen together” (Deuteronomy 22:11) may, like some other laws of a similar character, have been intended to express symbolically the separateness and simplicity of God’s covenant people. The wool of Damascus, famous for its whiteness, was of great repute in the Tyrian market (Ezekiel 27:18).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BATHS The use of the bath was very frequent among the Hebrews (Leviticus 14:8; Numbers 19:19, ect.). The high priest at his inauguration (Leviticus 8:6), and on the day of atonement, was required to bathe himself (16:4, 24). The “pools” mentioned in Nehemiah 3:15, 16, 2 Kings 20:20, Isaiah 22:11, John 9:7, were public bathing-places.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). LOG the smallest measure for liquids used by the Hebrews (Leviticus 14:10, 12, 15, 21, 24), called in the Vulgate sextarius. It is the Hebrew unit of measure of capacity, and is equal to the contents of six ordinary hen’s eggs=the twelfth part of a him, or nearly a pint.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). TENTH DEAL i.e., the tenth part of an ephah (as in the R.V.), equal to an omer or six pints. The recovered leper, to complete his purification, was required to bring a trespass, a sin, and a burnt offering, and to present a meal offering, a tenth deal or an omer of flour for each, with oil to make it into bread or cakes (Leviticus 14:10, 21; comp. Exodus 16:36; 29:40).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DWELLINGS The materials used in buildings were commonly bricks, sometimes also stones (Leviticus 14:40, 42), which were held together by cement (Jeremiah 43:9) or bitumen (Genesis 11:3). The exterior was usually whitewashed (Leviticus 14:41; Ezekiel 13:10; Matthew 23:27). The beams were of sycamore (Isaiah 9:10), or olive-wood, or cedar (1 Kings 7:2; Isaiah 9:10). The form of Eastern dwellings differed in many respects from that of dwellings in Western lands. The larger houses were built in a quadrangle enclosing a court-yard (Luke 5:19; 2 Samuel 17:18; Nehemiah 8:16) surrounded by galleries, which formed the guest-chamber or reception-room for visitors. The flat roof, surrounded by a low parapet, was used for many domestic and social purposes. It was reached by steps from the court. In connection with it (2 Kings 23:12) was an upper room, used as a private chamber (2 Sam 18:33; Daniel 6:11), also as a bedroom (2 Kings 23:12), a sleeping apartment for guests (2 Kings 4:10), and as a sick-chamber (1 Kings 17:19). The doors, sometimes of stone, swung on morticed pivots, and were generally fastened by wooden bolts. The houses of the more wealthy had a doorkeeper or a female porter (John 18:16; Acts 12:13). The windows generally opened into the courtyard, and were closed by a lattice (Judges 5:28). The interior rooms were set apart for the female portion of the household. The furniture of the room (2 Kings 4:10) consisted of a couch furnished with pillows (Amos 6:4; Ezekiel 13:20); and besides this, chairs, a table and lanterns or lamp-stands (2 Kings 4:10).
